Those who said this:

17781 – Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, saying: My paternal uncle narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn Abbas: ﴿So none believed in Musa except a few [dhurriyyah] of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, that he would persecute them﴾, he said: The dhurriyyah who believed in Musa were from people other than the Children of Israel, from the people of Pharaoh, a small number, among them: Pharaoh's wife, the believer of Pharaoh's family, Pharaoh's treasurer, and his treasurer's wife.

* *

A report has been transmitted from Ibn Abbas that indicates the opposite of this view, namely:

17782 – al-Muthanna narrated to me, saying: Abu Salih narrated to us, saying: Mu'awiyah narrated to me, from 'Ali, from Ibn Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿a dhurriyyah of his people﴾, he said: the Children of Israel.

* *

=This report indicates that he held that the "dhurriyyah" in this place [in the printed edition: "indicates it", and I have kept what is in the manuscript] are the Children of Israel, and not others from the people of Pharaoh.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most preferable of these views to me regarding the interpretation of the verse is the view I mentioned from Mujahid, namely that "dhurriyyah" in this place is intended to mean the descendants of those to whom Musa was sent from the Children of Israel, who died before acknowledging his prophethood because of the long passage of time, so their descendants reached adulthood, and among them whoever Allah guided believed in Musa.

I only said "this view is more correct in that," because no mention of anyone other than Musa has occurred in this verse. So for the pronoun in His words "from his people" to refer to the mention of Musa, since it is closer to his mention, is more preferable than that it refers to the mention of Pharaoh, since his mention is distant from it, and there is no evidence to the contrary, either from report or reasoning.

Furthermore, in His words ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾ there is clear evidence that the pronoun in His words ﴿except a few of his people﴾ refers to the mention of Musa, not the mention of Pharaoh, because if it referred to Pharaoh the speech would have been "out of fear of him," and it would not have been "out of fear of Pharaoh."

* *

As for His words ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh﴾, it means: in a state of fear of those among the descendants of Musa's people who believed in Musa. So the meaning of the speech is: none believed in Musa except a few of his people, from the Children of Israel, while they were fearful of Pharaoh and their chiefs that they would persecute them.

* *

Some of the grammarians of Arabic have claimed that it was only said "none believed in Musa except a few of his people" because those who believed in him had mothers from the Children of Israel and fathers from the Copts, so they were called "dhurriyyah" for this reason, just as the sons of the Persians whose mothers were Arab and whose fathers were non-Arab are called "abna'" (sons). [[This is al-Farra' in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:476.]]

The known meaning of "dhurriyyah" in the speech of the Arabs is: the offspring of the one to whom they are attributed, through men and women alike, as He, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿the offspring of those whom We carried with Noah﴾ [Surah al-Isra': 3], and as He said: ﴿And among his offspring [dhurriyyatihi] were Dawud, Sulayman, Ayyub, and Yusuf﴾, then He said after: ﴿and Zakariyya, Yahya, 'Isa, and Ilyas﴾ [Surah al-An'am: 84, 85], so He made those who were from the men and women the offspring of Ibrahim.

* *

As for His words ﴿and their chiefs [mala'ihim]﴾, "al-mala'" means: the nobles. [[See the explanation of "al-mala'" earlier, p. 155, footnote 1, and the references there.]] The meaning of the speech is: out of fear of Pharaoh and of their nobles.

* *

The people of Arabic differed regarding whom the "ha'" and "mim" in His words ﴿mala'ihim﴾ refer to. Some of the grammarians of Basra said: they refer to the dhurriyyah. It seems he directed the speech to: ﴿So none believed in Musa except a few of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh﴾ and the chiefs of the dhurriyyah from the Children of Israel.

* *

Some of the grammarians of Kufa said [in the printed edition: "grammarians of Kufa," and I have kept the manuscript reading]:

They refer to Pharaoh. He said: This is permissible although Pharaoh is one person, because when the king is mentioned in connection with fear, travel, or arrival from a journey, the thought goes to him and to those with him. He said: Do you not see that you say: "The caliph arrived, so the people multiplied," meaning those with him; and "he arrived, so prices rose," because by his arrival you intend the arrival of those with him. [[In the printed edition: "because we intend by his arrival..." and in the manuscript: "because we intend by his arrival and the arrival of those with him," which is an error; I have kept what is in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an.]]

* *

He said: It may also be that you mean by "Pharaoh" the family of Pharaoh, and omit "the family," [in the printed edition: "and omit"; in the manuscript: "so omit the family of Pharaoh," which is an error; the correct reading is from Ma'ani al-Qur'an] and it is permissible, as He said: ﴿and ask the town﴾ [Surah Yunus: 82], meaning the people of the town, and Allah knows best. He said: Similar to it is His words: ﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them for their waiting period﴾ [Surah al-Talaq: 1]. [[This preceding passage is the text of al-Farra's statement in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:476, 477.]]

* *

As for His words ﴿that he would persecute them﴾, it means: the belief of those who believed among the descendants of Musa's people was out of fear of Pharaoh, "that he would persecute them" with punishment, so that he would turn them away from their religion and compel them to return from their faith and disbelieve in Allah. [[See the explanation of "al-fitnah" earlier in the index of linguistic terms (f-t-n).]]

He said: ﴿that he would persecute them﴾ in the singular, and did not say "that they would persecute them," because the report about Pharaoh indicates it: that his people were in the same state as he was, due to what preceded in His words: ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs﴾.

* *

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verses 82–83:

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah will establish the truth by His words, even if the criminals dislike it﴾ (82)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, is informing about Musa that he said to the magicians: ﴿And Allah will establish the truth﴾, meaning: Allah will confirm the truth that I have brought you from Him, so He will make it prevail over your falsehood and make it sound. "By His words" means: by His command [[See the explanation of "yuhiqq al-haqq bi-kalimatihi" earlier, 13:407, footnotes 2, 3, and the references there.]] ﴿even if the criminals dislike it﴾, meaning those who earned sin against their Lord [[See the explanation of the meaning of "atham bi-rabbihi" earlier, p. 155, footnote 3, and the references there.]] by their disobedience to Him.

* *

On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿But none believed in Musa except a few [dhurriyyah] of his people, out of fear of Pharaoh and their chiefs, that he would persecute them. Indeed, Pharaoh was haughty in the land, and indeed he was among the transgressors﴾ (83)

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: So none believed in Musa, despite the proofs and evidences that came to them, ﴿except a few [dhurriyyah] of his people﴾, fearing Pharaoh and their chiefs.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And Moses said, 'O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims.'" (10:84)**

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, the One who is remembered, says, reporting what His prophet Moses said to his people: "O my people, if you have acknowledged the oneness of Allah and affirmed His lordship," then "rely upon Him" means: trust in Him and submit to His command. [[See the explanation of "al-tawakkul" (reliance) above, p. 147, note 5, and the references there.]]

For He will not forsake His ally, and whoever relies upon Him will not be left unsatisfied. [[In the printed edition: "wa yuslam" (and he will be safe); in the manuscript: "wa lam yuslam" (and he was not safe). The correct reading is what has been adopted.]] "If you are Muslims" means: if you are submitting to Allah in obedience, then rely upon Him. [[See the explanation of "al-Islam" in the earlier lexical indexes, under (s-l-m).]]

* *

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "So they said, 'In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.' (10:85)"**

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, the One who is remembered, says: The people said to Moses, "In Allah we have put our trust," meaning: in Him we have placed our confidence, and to Him we have entrusted our affair.

* *

As for His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": Allah, whose praise is great, reports about the people of Moses that they called upon their Lord and said: "O our Lord, do not test these disbelieving people through us, and do not put them to trial by means of us!" [[See the explanation of "al-fitnah" (trial) in the earlier lexical indexes, under (f-t-n).]] That is, they meant the people of Pharaoh.

* *

The interpreters have differed concerning the meaning of what they asked their Lord to protect them from, namely that Pharaoh's people should be tried by them.

Some of them said: They asked Him not to let them prevail over them, lest they think that they were better than them, and that they had been empowered over them only because of their own honor before Him and the humiliation of the others.

Those who said this:

17783 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr, from Abū Mijlaz, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not let them prevail over us, so that they think they are better than us."

17784 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥajjāj narrated to us, saying: Ḥammād narrated to us, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr, from Abū Mijlaz, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "They said: Do not make them prevail over us, so that they think they are better than us."

17785 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyān, from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā, regarding "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not empower them over us, so that they increase in trial."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: Do not empower them over us, so that they tempt us.

Those who said this:

17786 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not empower them over us, so that they tempt us."

17787 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Ibn ʿUyayna, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not empower them over us, so that they lead us astray."

17788 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna informed us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the same, and he also said: "so that they tempt us."

17789 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not punish us at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished,' and so they are tempted by us."

17790 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, his words: "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," he said: "Do not punish us at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished,' and so they are tempted by us."

17791 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Ḥakkām narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza, from Mujāhid, his words: "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," he said: "Do not afflict us with a punishment from You, nor at their hands, so that they are tempted and say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished.'"

17792 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not test us, our Lord, so that we are distressed and he makes it a trial for them. This is the trial." And he recited: "a trial for the wrongdoers" [Surah al-Ṣāffāt: 63], and said: The polytheists, when they used to harm the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers and hurl insults at them, said: "Is that not a trial for them and an evil for them, while it is an affliction for the believers?"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is that it should be said: The people sought refuge with Allah that He would protect them from becoming a test and an affliction for Pharaoh's people. Everything that happened to them that would have turned them away from following Moses, acknowledging him, and believing in what he brought them, was undoubtedly a "trial" for them, and among the greatest of matters that would have kept them far from faith in Allah and His messenger. Likewise, among the things that would have turned them away from faith was that, if the people of Moses were quickly struck by an affliction from Allah in their own persons, some calamity descending upon them. So the people sought refuge with Allah from every meaning that would have diverted Pharaoh's people from faith in Allah, by its causes.

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "And Moses said, 'O my people, if you have believed in Allah, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims.'" (10:84)**

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, the One who is remembered, says, reporting what His prophet Moses said to his people: "O my people, if you have acknowledged the oneness of Allah and affirmed His lordship," then "rely upon Him" means: trust in Him and submit to His command. [[See the explanation of "al-tawakkul" (reliance) above, p. 147, note 5, and the references there.]]

For He will not forsake His ally, and whoever relies upon Him will not be left unsatisfied. [[In the printed edition: "wa yuslam" (and he will be safe); in the manuscript: "wa lam yuslam" (and he was not safe). The correct reading is what has been adopted.]] "If you are Muslims" means: if you are submitting to Allah in obedience, then rely upon Him. [[See the explanation of "al-Islam" in the earlier lexical indexes, under (s-l-m).]]

* *

**Commentary on the words of Allah, the Exalted: "So they said, 'In Allah we have put our trust. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.' (10:85)"**

Abu Ja'far said: Allah, the One who is remembered, says: The people said to Moses, "In Allah we have put our trust," meaning: in Him we have placed our confidence, and to Him we have entrusted our affair.

* *

As for His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": Allah, whose praise is great, reports about the people of Moses that they called upon their Lord and said: "O our Lord, do not test these disbelieving people through us, and do not put them to trial by means of us!" [[See the explanation of "al-fitnah" (trial) in the earlier lexical indexes, under (f-t-n).]] That is, they meant the people of Pharaoh.

* *

The interpreters have differed concerning the meaning of what they asked their Lord to protect them from, namely that Pharaoh's people should be tried by them.

Some of them said: They asked Him not to let them prevail over them, lest they think that they were better than them, and that they had been empowered over them only because of their own honor before Him and the humiliation of the others.

Those who said this:

17783 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr, from Abū Mijlaz, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not let them prevail over us, so that they think they are better than us."

17784 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: al-Ḥajjāj narrated to us, saying: Ḥammād narrated to us, from ʿImrān ibn Ḥudayr, from Abū Mijlaz, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "They said: Do not make them prevail over us, so that they think they are better than us."

17785 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: My father narrated to us, from Sufyān, from his father, from Abū al-Ḍuḥā, regarding "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not empower them over us, so that they increase in trial."

* *

Others said: Rather, the meaning of that is: Do not empower them over us, so that they tempt us.

Those who said this:

17786 – Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not empower them over us, so that they tempt us."

17787 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Isḥāq narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Zubayr narrated to us, from Ibn ʿUyayna, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," that he said: "Do not empower them over us, so that they lead us astray."

17788 – al-Ḥasan ibn Yaḥyā narrated to us, saying: ʿAbd al-Razzāq informed us, saying: Ibn ʿUyayna informed us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, the same, and he also said: "so that they tempt us."

17789 – al-Muthannā narrated to me, saying: Abū Ḥudhayfa narrated to us, saying: Shibl narrated to us, from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from Mujāhid, regarding "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not punish us at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished,' and so they are tempted by us."

17790 – al-Qāsim narrated to us, saying: al-Ḥusayn narrated to us, saying: Ḥajjāj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujāhid, his words: "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," he said: "Do not punish us at the hands of Pharaoh's people, nor with a punishment from You, so that Pharaoh's people say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished,' and so they are tempted by us."

17791 – Ibn Ḥumayd narrated to us, saying: Ḥakkām narrated to us, from ʿAnbasa, from Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from al-Qāsim ibn Abī Bazza, from Mujāhid, his words: "Do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people," he said: "Do not afflict us with a punishment from You, nor at their hands, so that they are tempted and say: 'If they were upon the truth, we would not have been empowered over them, nor would they have been punished.'"

17792 – Yūnus narrated to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said regarding His words, "Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people": "Do not test us, our Lord, so that we are distressed and he makes it a trial for them. And he recited: "a trial for the wrongdoers" [Surah al-Ṣāffāt: 63], and said: The polytheists, when they used to harm the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers and hurl insults at them, said: "Is that not a trial for them and an evil for them, while it is an affliction for the believers?"

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view on this matter is that it should be said: The people sought refuge with Allah that He would protect them from becoming a test and an affliction for Pharaoh's people. Everything that happened to them that would have turned them away from following Moses, acknowledging him, and believing in what he brought them, was undoubtedly a "trial" for them, and among the greatest of matters that would have kept them far from faith in Allah and His messenger. Likewise, among the things that would have turned them away from faith was that, if the people of Moses were quickly struck by an affliction from Allah in their own persons, some calamity descending upon them. So the people sought refuge with Allah from every meaning that would have diverted Pharaoh's people from faith in Allah, by its causes.

* *

Others said: the meaning of that is: "Make your houses face one another."

Those who said that:

17818. Ibn Wakī' narrated to us, saying: Imran ibn Uyaynah narrated to us, from Ata', from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾, he said: "Facing one another."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings is the one we have already explained, because the most common meaning of "houses" (even though mosques are houses), when mentioned by its unrestricted name without being linked to anything or attributed to anything, is inhabited houses. That is because "mosques" have a name by which they are known, specific to them, namely "mosques." As for "houses" in unrestricted form, not attached to anything else nor attributed to anything, it means inhabited houses.

Likewise, "qiblah" is most commonly used by people for the direction of mosques and for prayers.

Since this is so, and since it is not permissible to direct the meanings of God's speech except to the most common of its senses, as used among the people of the language in which it was revealed, and not to the obscure and unknown, unless there is an indication that points to something else (and there is no indication regarding His words ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ that definitively removes the excuse that its meaning differs from the apparent sense used in Arabic speech), then it is not permissible for us to direct it to other than the apparent sense we have described.

The same applies to His words "qiblah."

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The most correct of these sayings is the one we have already explained, because the most common meaning of "houses" (even though mosques are houses), when mentioned by its unrestricted name without being linked to anything or attributed to anything, is inhabited houses. That is because "mosques" have a name by which they are known, specific to them, namely "mosques." As for "houses" in unrestricted form, not attached to anything else nor attributed to anything, it means inhabited houses.

Likewise, "qiblah" is most commonly used by people for the direction of mosques and for prayers.

Since this is so, and since it is not permissible to direct the meanings of God's speech except to the most common of its senses, as used among the people of the language in which it was revealed, and not to the obscure and unknown, unless there is an indication that points to something else (and there is no indication regarding His words ﴿and make your houses a qiblah﴾ that definitively removes the excuse that its meaning differs from the apparent sense used in Arabic speech), then it is not permissible for us to direct it to other than the apparent sense we have described.

The same applies to His words "qiblah."

* *

﴿And establish prayer﴾: He, exalted is His remembrance, means: "Perform the obligatory prayer with its limits at its times." [See the explanation of "establishing prayer" in the preceding lexical indexes, under (q-w-m).]

As for His words ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾: He, exalted is His praise, says to His Prophet, peace be upon him: "And give good tidings, O Muhammad, to those who establish prayer and obey God, the believers, of His abundant reward." [See the explanation of "tabshir" (giving good tidings) in what preceded, p. 124, note 2, and the references there.]

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verse 88:

The interpretation of His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chieftains splendor and wealth in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead [people] astray from Your way. Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts, so that they will not believe until they see the painful punishment."﴾ (10:88)

Abu Ja'far said: He, may His remembrance be exalted, says: Moses said, "O our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and the great men of his people and their nobles" [see the explanation of "al-mala'" (the chieftains) earlier, p. 166, note 2, and the references there] — they are "al-mala'" — "splendor" (zinah), from the goods and furnishings of the world [see the explanation of "al-zinah" earlier, 12:389] — ﴿and wealth﴾ in the form of gold and silver ingots — ﴿in the life of this world. Our Lord, that they may lead [people] astray from Your way.﴾ Moses says to his Lord: "Our Lord, You gave them what You gave them of that so that they would lead [people] astray from Your way."

* *

The reciters differed regarding the reading of this.

Some of them read: ﴿liyudilloo 'an sabilik﴾ [li-yuḍillū], meaning: that they may lead the people astray from Your way and turn them away from Your religion.

* *

Others read it: ﴿liyaḍillū 'an sabilik﴾ [li-yaḍillū], meaning: that they themselves may go astray from Your way and deviate from the path of guidance. [See these two readings in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:477.]

* *

If someone says: Did God, may His praise be exalted, give Pharaoh and his people what He gave them of the splendor and wealth of this world so that they would lead people astray from His religion, or so that they themselves would go astray from it? If He gave it to them for that purpose, then what He gave them was for that, [in the printed edition: "what He gave for its sake," and I have kept what is in the manuscript], so there is no blame upon them for that? It is said: The meaning of that is contrary to what you suppose. [In the manuscript, the copyist omitted and wrote: "so there is no blame upon them for that, contrary to what you suppose," and the editor of the printed edition was correct in what he inferred from the context.]

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed regarding the meaning of this "lam" in His saying: ﴿liyudilloo﴾ [liyuḍillū].

Some grammarians of Basra said: The meaning is: "Our Lord, they went astray from Your way," as in His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a grief﴾ (28:8) — that is, so it became for them [an enemy]; they did not pick him up so that he would become an enemy and grief for them, but they picked him up and it became so for them. He said: This "lam" comes in this sense. [That is, the sense of consequence and outcome.]

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: This "lam" is "lam of kay" [the lam of purpose]. [This is al-Farra in Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:477.] The meaning of the speech is: "Our Lord, I gave them what I gave them, so that they would go astray," then He invoked against them.

* *

Another said: These "lams" in His saying ﴿liyudilloo﴾ and ﴿liyakūna lahum 'aduwwan﴾ and what is similar to them are, in interpretation, the "lam" of attribution: "I gave them what I gave them for their going astray," and "they picked him up for his becoming..." — the situation had come to that. The Arabs make the "lam of kay" serve the meaning of the "lam of attribution" and the "lam of attribution" serve the meaning of the "lam of kay," due to the closeness of meaning. God, may He be exalted, says: ﴿They will swear to you by God when you return to them, that you may turn away from them﴾ (9:95) — that is, for your turning away; they did not swear for their own turning away. And a poet said: [I do not know who said it.]

You rose, though you were not fit to rise,
but the one who wastes [his gifts] is sometimes struck.

He said: It is said, "And I was not fit for the act," and it is rarely said "to act." He said: This is one such case.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter, in my opinion, is that it is the "lam of kay" — and the meaning of the speech is: "Our Lord, I gave them what I gave them of the splendor of the life of this world and wealth, so that You might test them through it and that they would lead Your servants astray from Your way, as a punishment from You." This is like His, may His praise be exalted, saying: ﴿Had they remained upon the path, We would have given them abundant water, that We might test them therein﴾ (72:16–17).

* *

As for His saying: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts﴾ — this is a supplication from Moses, invoking God against Pharaoh and his chiefs, that He change their wealth from its form and transform it into a state other than that in which it is. This is like His saying: ﴿before We obliterate faces and turn them back upon their backs﴾ (4:47). He means by it: before We change them from the form in which they are.

* *

It is said from this: "I obliterated his eye, I obliterate it, and I obliterate it obliteration and effacement." The Arabs use "al-tamas" (obliteration) for erasure and effacement, and for crushing and obliteration, as Ka'b ibn Zuhayr said:

From every sweating, wide-necked [camel] when she perspires,
her trappings are faded of their marks, unknown.

* *

The interpreters differed regarding the interpretation of this in this place. A group of them said the same as what we have said.

[Report 17845: "al-Minqari," thus in the printed edition. In the manuscript it is "al-Ma'arri," written without dots, and I have been unable to determine whom it means.]

* *

The grammarians differed regarding the position of ﴿yu'minu﴾ [yu'minū].

Some grammarians of Basra said: It is in the subjunctive, because the response to the imperative is with the fa', or it is an invocation against them since they disobeyed. It has been related from the sayer of this view that he used to say: it is in the subjunctive, conjoined to His saying ﴿that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾.

* *

Another of them [this is Abu 'Ubayda in Majaz al-Qur'an 1:281], and this is the view of the grammarians of Kufa: its position is the jussive, as an invocation from Moses against them, meaning: "so they did not believe," as the poet said: [this is al-A'sha]:

So let there not be spread between your eyes what has been drawn together,
and do not meet me except with your nose in the dust.

[Diwan: 58, from his poem in satire of Yazid ibn Mus-hir al-Shaybani, in which he says to him: ...]

The meaning: "so let not what has been drawn together between your eyes be spread out," and "do not meet me," as an invocation.

* *

Some grammarians of Kufa said: It is an invocation, as though he said: "O God, so let them not believe." He said: And if you wish, you may make it the answer to his request, since the request came in the form of an imperative, so ﴿so they will not believe﴾ is in the subjunctive position as an answer, but it is not easy. He said: It would be like the poet's saying: [this is Abu al-Najm]:

O she-camel, travel a wide, spacious gait
to Sulayman, that we may rest.

He said: The answer is not easy in supplication, because it is not a condition.

* *

Abu Ja'far said: The correct view in this matter is that it is in the jussive position, as an invocation, meaning: "so let them not believe." I chose this because what precedes it is an invocation, namely His saying: ﴿Our Lord, obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts﴾, so attaching ﴿so they will not believe﴾ to that context, being in its sense, is more fitting and more appropriate.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿until they see the painful punishment﴾, Ibn Abbas used to say: its meaning is: until they see the drowning. We have already mentioned the report from him to that effect, in some of its channels, earlier.

17846 - al-Qasim told me, saying: al-Husayn told us, saying: Hajjaj told me, from Ibn Jurayj, Ibn Abbas said: ﴿so they will not believe until they see the painful punishment﴾, he said: "The drowning."

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verse 89:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He said: "Your supplication has been answered, so go straight and do not follow the way of those who do not know."﴾

Abu Ja'far said: This is information from God about His answering the supplication of Musa (ﷺ) and Harun for [the destruction of] Pharaoh, the chiefs of his people, and their wealth. His majestic praise says: ﴿He said﴾, that is, God said to them: ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾, concerning Pharaoh, his council, and their wealth.

* *

If someone says: How is "answering" attributed to two when "supplication" came from only one?

It is said: Although the one who supplicated was one, the second was one who said "Amin" (mu'ammin), and he was Harun. Therefore the answering is attributed to both of them, because the one who says amin is a supplicant (da'in). [[See al-Farra', Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1: 478.]] And so did the people of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) say.

Mention of those who said that:

17847 - Muhammad ibn Bashshar related to me, saying: 'Abd al-Rahman related to us, saying: Sufyan related to us, from Ibn Jurayj, from a man, from Ikrimah, concerning His saying: ﴿Your supplication has been answered﴾, he said: Musa would supplicate, and Harun would say amin, and that is His saying: ﴿Your supplications have been answered﴾.

* *

Some scholars of Arabic have claimed that the Arabs address one person with the address of two, and they recited in support of this: [[He is Mudarris ibn Rab'i al-Asadi.]]

Then I said to my companion: "Do not hasten us
with uprooting its roots, and cut off the shih (wormwood)."

[Editor's note on the verse: the poem is cited in al-Sahibi, Ibn Ya'ish, and al-Lisan, and it is from a longer poem of his about roasting meat; its variants are noted in the original, and the rest of the bracketed note explains the vocabulary: "al-najih" is swift glory; "al-ya'malat" are she-camels; "al-dawami" are those whose hands have bled from long, hard travel; "al-sarih" are rags or hides tied on the hooves of camels when they bleed. The speaker tells his companion not to keep them waiting with a long delay in pulling up the firewood from its roots, but to take whatever easily available sticks and branches and bring them so they can roast the meat.]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿so go straight﴾, it is a command from God to Musa and Harun to be steadfast and firm in their affair, from calling Pharaoh and his people to accept the worship of God and obedience to Him, until the punishment of God comes upon them, of which He informed them that He had answered them. [[See the explanation of "istiqamah" in the earlier lexical indexes (qawm).]] As:

17856 - al-Qasim related to us, saying: al-Husayn related to us, saying: Hajjaj related to me, who said: Ibn Jurayj said, Ibn 'Abbas said: ﴿so go straight﴾: proceed with My command, and that is istiqamah. Ibn Jurayj said: They say that Pharaoh remained forty years after this supplication. [[Thus in the printed edition and al-Durr al-Manthur: "after this supplication"; in the manuscript: "after this verse," though "verse" is poorly written.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿and do not follow the way of those who do not know﴾, [[See the explanation of "ittiba'" and "sabil" in the earlier lexical indexes (tb'), (sbl), and what comes shortly in the interpretation of the next verse.]] it means: and do not take the path of those who are ignorant of the reality of My promise, so that you hasten My decree. For My promise has no reversal, and My threat will descend upon Pharaoh, and My punishment will befall him and his people.

**Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on Surah 10, verse 90:**

**On the interpretation of His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea, and Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them in insolence and enmity, until when drowning overtook him he said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾**

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: His mention, exalted is He, means: We divided the sea for the Children of Israel until they crossed it [[See the explanation of "jawaza" (crossed) above, 5:345 / 13:80.]] = ﴿Then Pharaoh followed them﴾, meaning: Pharaoh followed them ﴿with his hosts﴾.

It is said that the verb is used as "atba'tuhu" and "tabi'tuhu," with the same meaning.

al-Kisa'i, as Abu 'Ubayd reported from him, used to say: when one means that he followed them for good or for evil, the wording is "atba'ahum," with a hamza on the alif. When one means that he followed their track or took them as an example, it is from "ittaba'tu," with the taa' doubled and the alif unhamzated.

* *

﴿In insolence﴾ against Musa, Harun, and those with them from their people, the Children of Israel [[See the explanation of "al-baghy" (insolence) above, p. 53, note 2, and the references there.]] = ﴿and enmity﴾, meaning: and aggression against them.

* *

It is a verbal noun from their saying: "So-and-so transgressed (ʿadā) against so-and-so in wrongdoing, transgressing against him, ʿadwan," like "ghazā yaghzū ghazwan." [[See the explanation of "al-ʿudwān" (transgression) above, 14:151, note 4, and the references there.]]

* *

It has been reported from some of them that he read: ﴿baghyan wa ʿudwan﴾, and this is likewise a verbal noun from their saying: "ʿadā yaʿdū ʿudwan," like "ʿalā yaʿlū ʿuluwwan." [[See what has preceded, 12:35, 36.]]

* *

= ﴿Until when drowning overtook him﴾, meaning: until when drowning encompassed him. [[See the explanation of "al-idrāk" (overtaking) above, 12:13–21.]] = There is an omitted element in the speech, which has been left out because what appears of the speech indicates it. It is: "Pharaoh followed them with his hosts in insolence and enmity," [so We drowned him] = ﴿until when drowning overtook him﴾.

* *

As for His words: ﴿He said: "I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾, the mention, exalted is He, is reporting what Pharaoh said when he was on the brink of drowning, [[In the printed edition: "ashraf ʿalā al-gharq" (overlooked drowning). The editor did not read the manuscript well, since it is unpointed; the correct reading is what has been established. "Ashfā ʿalā al-mawt aw ghayrihi" means he came close to it, from "al-shafā," which is the edge of anything.]] and was certain of destruction: ﴿I believe﴾, meaning: I acknowledge, ﴿that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe.﴾

* *

The readers differed regarding the recitation of this.

Some of them read it, and this is the reading of the majority of Madina and Basra: ﴿أَنَّهُ﴾ with the alif of "annahu" opened (fatha), governed by "āmantu" and put in the accusative by it.

* *

Others read: ﴿āmantu innahu﴾ with the alif of "innahu" kasra, on the basis of beginning the predicate. This is the reading of the majority of the Kufans. [[See these two readings in al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:478.]]

* *

My view on this is that they are two readings close in meaning, and whichever of them the reciter reads, he is correct.

* *

Those concerned with interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) also said something similar to what we have said.

Those who said this:

17857. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Yahya ibn Wadih narrated to us, saying: Musa ibn Ubayda narrated to us, from Muhammad ibn Ka'b, from Abdullah ibn Shaddad, who said: Ya'qub and his sons gathered with Yusuf, and they were seventy-two. And they went out with Musa from Egypt when they went out, and they were six hundred thousand. When Pharaoh overtook them and they saw him, they said: "O Musa, where is the way out? For he has overtaken us. We used to suffer trials from Pharaoh!" So God revealed to Musa: "Strike the sea with your staff," and it split, and every part became like a great mountain, [[A quotation from the verse of Surah al-Shu'ara' 26:63.]] and the sea dried up for them, and God uncovered the face of the earth. Pharaoh came out on a dark bay steed, of a color among the dark colors, with eight hundred thousand (horsemen), apart from their other mounts. Under Jibril, peace be upon him, was a mare in heat, with no female in it besides her, [["Wadiq": a mare in heat, desiring the stallion. See what has preceded, 2:52.]] and Mika'il was driving them, so that no man of them strayed except that he joined him to the people. When the last of the Children of Israel came out, Jibril approached him and clung to him, and the stallion found the scent of the female, and Pharaoh could not control his affair at all. And he said: "Advance! The people have no more right to the sea than you!" Then Pharaoh followed them, until when their first ones were about to come out, he sank and called out: ﴿"I believe that there is no god except the One in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of those who submit."﴾ And it was said to him: ﴿"Now? And you had disobeyed before, and you were among the corrupters."﴾

17858. Muhammad ibn al-Muthanna narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Ja'far narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas: =

= And from Adi ibn Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, who said, raising it to the Prophet ﷺ: "Indeed Jibril used to stuff the mud into the mouth of Pharaoh, lest he say: 'There is no god but God.'" [[The two reports: 17858, 17859. The report of Ibn Abbas was narrated by Ahmad through this route, the route of Shu'ba, from Adi ibn Thabit and Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, in his Musnad, numbers 2144, 3154. Abu Dawud al-Tayalisi narrated it in his Musnad, p. 341, number 2618.

al-Hakim narrated it in al-Mustadrak 2:340, and said: "This is a sound hadith according to the condition of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), though they did not record it, except that most of Shu'ba's companions stopped it at Ibn Abbas," and al-Dhahabi agreed with him. See the stopped version below: 17865. It was narrated by al-Tirmidhi in the Book of Tafsir, and he said: "Hasan gharib sahih."

See below, number 17862.]]

17859. al-Husayn ibn Amr ibn Muhammad al-Anqazi narrated to me, saying: My father narrated to us, saying: Shu'ba narrated to us, from Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib, from Adi ibn Thabit, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, who said: "Jibril, peace be upon him, began to stuff = or: to fill = into the mouth of Pharaoh the mud, lest the mercy overtake him."

17860. Ibn Humayd narrated to us, saying: Hakkam narrated to us, from Anbasa, from Kathir ibn Zadhan, from Abu Hazim, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Prophet ﷺ said: "Jibril said to me: 'O Muhammad, if you had seen me while I was pushing him under and stuffing the mud into his mouth, lest the mercy of God overtake him and He forgive him!'" = meaning Pharaoh. [[The report: 17860. "Hakkam" is Hakkam ibn Salm al-Kinani, trustworthy, but Ahmad said of him: "He was of good appearance, he came to us, and he used to narrate strange hadiths from Anbasa," already mentioned several times. "Anbasa" is Anbasa ibn Sa'id al-Darris, trustworthy, with no harm in him, already mentioned several times. "Kathir ibn Zadhan al-Nakha'i": Ibn Ma'in said: "I do not know him." Abu Hatim and Abu Zur'a said: "This is an unknown shaykh; we do not know anyone who narrated from him except what Ibn Humayd narrated from Harun ibn al-Mughira, from Anbasa, from him." He is biographed in al-Tahdhib, Ibn Abi Hatim 3/2/151, and Mizan al-I'tidal 2:353, where it is said: "From Asim ibn Damra, he has a munkar hadith."

"Abu Hazim" is Salman al-Ashja'i, trustworthy, already mentioned in number 7616.

So this report is very weak, due to the weakness of Kathir ibn Zadhan. al-Haythami cited something similar in Majma' al-Zawa'id 7:36, from Abu Hurayra, and said: "It was narrated by al-Tabarani in al-Awsat, and in it is Qays ibn al-Rabi', whom Shu'ba and al-Thawri trusted, but a group weakened him."

His words "aghtahu" mean: to immerse him in water and dip him. "Al-hal" is black mud and silt, which is "hal al-bahr" (the silt of the sea). In the printed edition it was "wa-hami'a" (and slime), other than what is in the manuscript, because its meaning was not known, so he thought it an error.]]

[[The report: 17861. "Ali ibn Zayd ibn Jud'an," already mentioned several times, the last being number 17154–17516. My brother, Sayyid Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, declared him trustworthy in the Musnad, number 783, and in what preceded of his notes on some hadiths of al-Tabari. But I have seen the imams weakening him (not that they accused him of lying), considering him closer to laxity, and that he used to reverse hadiths, and used to narrate a hadith one day and narrate it differently the next day, so he is not so reliable, and his memory was poor. I fear that my brother was rash in declaring him trustworthy, but I consider that his narrations are taken into account, and his hadiths are written, but he is not used as proof; Muslim only narrated from him in conjunction with others. This is the extent of Ali ibn Zayd in my view, and God knows best.

This report was narrated by Ahmad in his Musnad, number 2203, through the route of Yunus, from Hammad ibn Salama, and number 2821 through the route of Sulayman ibn Harb, from Hammad. My brother, may God have mercy on him, declared it sound in both places. al-Tirmidhi recorded it in the Book of Tafsir of his Sunan, through this same route, and said: "This is a hasan hadith." In the printed edition it was "akhudhu min hama't al-bahr" (I take from the mud of the sea), and I have established what is in the manuscript.

Its origin is "dassasahu," doubled, then the sins followed each other, and the last of them was changed into a ya'. Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verse 91–92:

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Now? And you had disobeyed before and were among the corrupters.﴾ (91)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says, informing Pharaoh of the ugliness of his conduct during his lifetime and of his harm to himself during his days of health, through his persistence in his transgression and his disobedience to his Lord, when he turned to Him in the state of His wrath descending upon him and His punishment coming down, seeking refuge with Him from the torment that had befallen him, when he called out while the waves of the sea had overtaken him and the agonies of death had enveloped him: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims.﴾ To Him, submitting in humility to Him, acknowledging servitude [to Him] — now you acknowledge servitude to God, submit to Him in humility, and devote divinity to Him, when you had disobeyed Him before the descent of His vengeance upon you, so you incurred His anger against yourself, and you were among the corrupters on earth, those who turned away from His way? Why did you not, while you were in respite and the door of repentance was open to you, acknowledge what you now acknowledge?

* *

The interpretation of His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So today We will save you in your body that you may be a sign to those who succeed you. And indeed, many of the people, of Our signs, are heedless.﴾ (92)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says to Pharaoh: Today We will place you on a high place of the earth in your body, so that one who denied your destruction may look at you as one destroyed. ﴿That you may be a sign to those who succeed you﴾ means: that you may be a lesson for those after you among the people, by which they take warning, so that they refrain from disobedience to God, from disbelief in Him, and from striving in His land with corruption.

= And "al-najwah" is the elevated place above what is around it from the earth, and from it is the saying of Aws ibn Hajar:

So whoever is in its courtyard is like whoever is on its elevation, and the one who hides is like the one who walks in the open sun [[From his Diwan, qasidah 4, verse 15, describing clouds and rain as severe, covering every place and every person. "Aqwat al-dar" is its courtyard and what surrounds it. "Al-mustakinn" is one who has hidden himself in a shelter. "Al-qirwah" is one who is exposed, with nothing to shield him from the sky and the sun.]]

17882. Ibn Wakic related to us, saying: al-Maharibi and Abu Khalid related to us, from Juwaybir, from al-Dahhak, regarding ﴿mubawwa' sidq﴾: he said: abodes of truthfulness, Egypt and Syria.

17883. Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-A'la related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr related to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatadah, regarding ﴿mubawwa' sidq﴾: he said: God settled them in Syria and Jerusalem.

17884. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding ﴿And We certainly settled the Children of Israel in a good settlement﴾: Syria. And he recited: ﴿to the land which We have blessed for the worlds﴾ [Surah al-Anbiya': 71].

* *

As for His words ﴿and provided them with good things﴾, He means: And We provided the Children of Israel with lawful provision, which is ﴿the good﴾. [[See the explanation of "al-tayyib" above in the language indices (tayyib).]]

* *

As for His words ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them﴾, His, the majestic one's, praise says: Those whom We did this to among the Children of Israel did not differ until there came to them what they had knowledge of. That is because before Muhammad, the Prophet ﷺ, was sent, they were agreed upon the prophethood of Muhammad and acknowledging him and his mission, not differing about it by the description which they found written among them. But when there came to them what they recognized, some of them disbelieved in it and some of them believed in it, and those among them who believed in it were a small number. This is His words: they did not differ until there came to them the known one whom they knew as a prophet of God. So "knowledge" was put in place of "the known."

* *

Some of them interpreted "knowledge" here as the Book of God and His revelation.

Mention of those who said that:

17885. Yunus related to me, saying: Ibn Wahb informed us, saying: Ibn Zayd said, regarding His words ﴿And they did not differ until knowledge had come to them﴾, [[In the printed and manuscript copies: "...until knowledge had come to them, out of rebellion among themselves," which is not part of the recitation of this verse, nor part of its explanation, so I have removed it. Similar verses in which mention of knowledge and rebellion regarding it occurs are in Surah Al 'Imran: 19; Surah al-Shura: 14; Surah al-Jathiyah: 17. I preferred to omit this addition from this place, because I did not find Abu Ja'far mentioning this report in the explanation of any of these verses, and the apparent meaning is that the meanings are taken from one another, so Ibn Zayd added to the explanation from parallels of the verse in other surahs.]] He said: "knowledge" is the Book of God which He sent down, and His command which He commanded them with. And did they differ until knowledge had come to them out of rebellion among themselves? Were not the people of these desires only fighting out of rebellion? He said: "Rebellion" has two aspects: the aspect of worldly prestige, and those who fight over it among its people; and rebellion in "knowledge," where one sees the other as ignorant and mistaken while seeing himself as correct and knowing, so he transgresses against that mistaken one with his correctness and knowledge.

* *

As for His words ﴿Indeed, your Lord will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection concerning that wherein they used to differ﴾, He, the Exalted, says to His Prophet Muhammad ﷺ: Indeed your Lord, O Muhammad, will judge between the disputing Children of Israel concerning you on the Day of Resurrection, concerning what they used to differ about in the world regarding My command, by admitting those among them who denied you to the Fire and those among them who believed in you to the Garden. That is His judgment on that Day concerning what they used to differ about regarding the matter of Muhammad ﷺ. [[See the explanation of "al-qada'" above in the language indices (qada).]]

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you. The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters.﴾ (10:94)

Abu Ja'far said: God, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): If you, O Muhammad, are in doubt about the reality of what We chose you for and sent down to you [[In the printed edition: "what We informed you of and sent down to you." I have adopted the correct reading from the manuscript.]], namely that the Children of Israel did not dispute your prophethood before you were sent as a messenger to His creation, because they find you written among them and recognise you by the description with which you are described in their Scripture, in the Torah and the Gospel, then ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾, from among the People of the Torah and the Gospel, such as ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and others like him, from among those of them who are truthful and who believe in you, not those of them who lie and disbelieve in you.

* *

Those who engage in ta'wil (exegesis) have said something similar to what we have said.

Those from among the People of the Scripture who met Muhammad (ﷺ) and believed in him." He means: ask them, if you are in doubt, that you are written down among them.

17888. Al-Qasim narrated to us, saying: al-Husayn narrated to us, saying: Hajjaj narrated to me, from Ibn Jurayj, from Mujahid, regarding His saying: ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾: "They are the People of the Scripture."

It was narrated to me from al-Husayn ibn al-Faraj, who said: I heard Abu Muʿadh say: ʿUbayd informed us, saying: I heard al-Dahhak say: ﴿ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾, meaning: the people of piety and the people of faith from among the People of the Scripture, those who met the Prophet of God (ﷺ).

* *

If someone says: Was the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in doubt about God's report that it is the absolute truth, such that it was said to him: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾?

It is said: No. This is also what a group of the people of knowledge said.

17890. Yaʿqub ibn Ibrahim narrated to me, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, from Abu Bishr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾, he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) did not doubt and did not ask."

17891. Ibn Waki' narrated to us, saying: Suwayd ibn ʿAmr narrated to us, from Abu ʿAwana, from Abu Bishr, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, regarding His saying: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾, he said: "He did not doubt and did not ask."

17892. al-Harith narrated to me, saying: al-Qasim ibn Salam narrated to us, saying: Hushaym narrated to us, saying: Abu Bishr informed us, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr = and Mansur, from al-Hasan, regarding this verse, he said: "He (ﷺ) did not doubt and did not ask."

17893. Bishr narrated to us, saying: Yazid narrated to us, saying: Saʿid narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His saying: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾: "It was mentioned to us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: I do not doubt and I do not ask."

17894. Muhammad ibn ʿAbd al-Aʿla narrated to us, saying: Muhammad ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Maʿmar, from Qatada: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, then ask those who have been reading the Scripture before you﴾, he said: "It reached us that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: I do not doubt and I do not ask."

* *

If someone says: Then what is the explanation of this statement, if the matter is as you have described? It is said: We have already explained in more than one place in this book that the Arabs permit a speaker among them to say to his slave: "If you are my slave, then come to my command," while the slave who is ordered to do so is not in doubt, nor is his master who says it to him, that he is his slave. Likewise a man among them says to his son: "If you are my son, then be dutiful to me," while he has no doubt about his son that he is his son. This is sound and widespread in their speech, and we have mentioned that with its evidence. Among it is God's saying: ﴿And when God says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides God'?"﴾ [Al-Ma'ida: 116], while He, exalted is His praise, knows that Jesus did not say that. [[See what has preceded at 11:236–237, and the Maʿani al-Qurʾan of al-Farra' 1:479.]] This is of that kind. The Prophet (ﷺ) was not doubting the reality or the truth of God's report, and God, exalted is His remembrance, knew that about His command. Rather, He, exalted is His praise, addressed him with the address of his people to one another, since the Qur'an was revealed in their tongue.

* *

As for His saying: ﴿The truth has certainly come to you from your Lord﴾, to the end of the verse, it is an independent report from God.

God, exalted is His remembrance, says: He swears: The true, certain news has certainly come to you that you are a messenger of God, and that these Jews and Christians know the soundness of that, and find your description with them in their books = ﴿so do not be among the doubters﴾, meaning: do not be among those who doubt its soundness and reality. [[See the explanation of "al-imtira'" (doubting) at 12:61, note 2, and the references there.]]

* *

If someone were to say: This verse was addressed to the Prophet (ﷺ), and what is meant by it is some of those whose insight into his prophethood (ﷺ) was not sound, from among those who had outwardly professed faith with their tongues, as a reminder to him of the point at which the reality of his matter is known, which removes confusion from his heart, just as God, exalted is His praise, said: ﴿O Prophet, fear God and do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Indeed God is ever Knowing and Wise﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 1], it would be a statement whose soundness is not refuted.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verse 95–97:

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And do not be among those who deny the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers﴾ (95).

Abu Ja'far (al-Tabari) said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says to His Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ): Do not be, O Muhammad, among those who deny the proofs and evidences of Allah, for you would then be among those whose share is diminished and who sell the mercy and pleasure of Allah for His wrath and punishment. [[See the explanation of "the verse" (ayah) in the earlier lexical indexes (ayy).

And see the explanation of "loss" (khusran) in the earlier lexical indexes (kh-s-r).]]

* *

The interpretation of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe (96). Even if every sign should come to them, until they see the painful punishment (97)﴾.

Abu Ja'far said: He, exalted is His remembrance, says: Indeed, those upon whom "the word of your Lord" has been due, O Muhammad, are those whom He cursed by His saying: ﴿Unquestionably, the curse of Allah is upon the wrongdoers﴾ [Surah Hud: 18], and so it became firmly established against them.

* *

It is said of it: "The matter is due upon so-and-so" (haqqa 'ala fulan kadhā yahuqqu 'alayhi), when it becomes established and obligatory for him.

[[See the explanation of "haqq" in the earlier pages, p. 85.]]

* *

As for His saying: ﴿They will not believe, even if every sign should come to them﴾, it means: they will not give credence to the proofs of Allah, nor acknowledge the oneness of their Lord, nor that you are the Messenger of Allah. ﴿Even if every sign should come to them﴾, and admonition and lesson, and they witness them, until they witness the painful punishment, just as Pharaoh and his chiefs did not believe when the word of your Lord was justified against them, until they witnessed the painful punishment. Then he said: ﴿I believe that there is no deity except the one in whom the Children of Israel have believed﴾ [Surah Yunus: 90], when his statement no longer benefited him. Likewise, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified from your people, among the worshippers of idols and others, will not believe in you so as to follow you, except at the moment when their belief will not benefit them.

* *

The people of interpretation have said what is similar to what we have said.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 10, verse 98:

The discussion of the interpretation of His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its belief benefited it, except the people of Yunus? When they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world, and We let them enjoy [their lives] for a time.﴾ (98)

Abu Ja'far said: He, the Exalted, says: "Why was there not a town that believed?" [[See "lawla" in the sense of "halla" (why not): 2:552, 553 / 11:266, 343, 356.]] And so it is, as is reported, in the reading of Ubayy.

The meaning of the speech is: No town believed when it witnessed the punishment and the descent of God's wrath upon it, because of its disobedience to its Lord and its deserving of His punishment, so that its belief at that time benefited it, just as the belief of Pharaoh did not benefit him when drowning overtook him after his persistence in his error and his deserving of God's wrath through his disobedience. ﴿Except the people of Yunus﴾: for their belief benefited them after the punishment had descended and the wrath had settled upon them.

God therefore excepted the people of Yunus from the people of the towns whose belief did not benefit them after the punishment had come into their courtyard, and He removed them from among them, and informed His creation that their belief benefited them specifically, out of all the other nations besides them.

* *

If someone says: If the matter is as you have described, that His saying ﴿Why was there not a town that believed, so that its belief benefited it﴾ means "No town believed," in the sense of denial, then how is "qawm" (people) in the accusative, when you know that if what precedes the exception is a negation, what follows it is in the nominative, and that the correct speech of the Arabs is: "No one stood up except your brother," and "No one went out except your father"?

It is said: That applies where what follows the exception is of the same kind as what precedes it, since "brother" is of the same kind as "anyone," and likewise "father." But if the two kinds differ, so that what follows the exception is not of the kind of what precedes it, the eloquent form in their speech is the accusative. This is like saying: "No one remained in the house except the peg (watad)," and "We have no one except a dog or a donkey," because "the dog," "the peg," and "the donkey" are not of the kind of "anyone." From this is the saying of al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani:

"He was unable to answer, and there was not in the enclosure any one [of them]"

Then he said:

"except the hearth-stones, hard to make out, whose wall-stones I clarify... and the trench like a basin in the wronged, hard ground."

So he put "al-awari" in the accusative, since it was excepted from something not of its kind. Likewise ﴿the people of Yunus﴾ is in the accusative, because they are a nation other than the nations from which they were excepted, and not of their kind or form, even though they are from the children of Adam. This is the exception which some grammarians call the disjunctive exception (al-istithna' al-munqati') [[See al-Farra's Ma'ani al-Qur'an 1:479, 480, which contains further explanation.]]. Had ﴿the people of Yunus﴾ been part of the "nation" from which they were excepted, the speech would have been in the nominative, but they are as you have described.

* *

Those who interpret the Qur'an have said the same as what we have said on this.

When God knew the sincerity in their hearts, and their repentance and remorse for what had passed from them, God removed the punishment from them after it had hung over them. He said: It was mentioned to us that the people of Yunus were at Nineveh, the land of Mosul.
